# Methods

## Study design and population

This study analyzed data from the prospective CoLaus\textbar{}PsyCoLaus cohort and its nested sub-study OsteoLaus. CoLaus is a population-based cohort of adults aged 35 to 75 years at baseline living in Lausanne, Switzerland, recruited between June 2003 and May 2006 at a single study centre. Follow-up assessments of the CoLaus cohort have been conducted across four waves: 2009-2013, 2014-2018, 2018-2021, and 2022-2026.

OsteoLaus is a sub-cohort nested within CoLaus, comprising women who participated in the CoLaus baseline examination and were invited to an additional study focused on bone health. The OsteoLaus study included $1\,475$ women aged 50 to 80 years at baseline and aimed to investigate fracture risk and the relationship between osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease [@shevroja2019].

Eligibility criteria for OsteoLaus included written informed consent, BMI between 15 and 40 kg/m², and availability of relevant skeletal measurement sites (vertebrae and femur), as well as data on previous osteoporotic fractures and heel ultrasound measurements. Women with known diseases affecting bone metabolism or skeletal sites were excluded.

Measurements were collected approximately every 2.5 years across five visits: baseline (2010-2012, n = $1\,475$), second visit (2012-2015, n = $1\,349$), third visit (2015-2018, n = $1\,242$), fourth visit (2017-2020, n = $1\,104$), and fifth visit (2020-2022, n = 944). Participants were mainly lost over time due to loss to follow-up, death, institutionalisation, refusal to participate, BMI above 40 kg/m², or severe psychiatric disease [@vendrami2025a].

Further details on recruitment and methodology for CoLaus and OsteoLaus are described by Firmann et al. [@firmann2008] and Shevroja et al. [@shevroja2019], respectively. Additional study information is available at the CoLaus\|PsyCoLaus [website](https://www.colaus-psycolaus.ch/). @fig-timeline shows the study population, visit timeline, and the variables collected at each visit.

![Overview of visit timeline](images/Study%20Overview.png){#fig-timeline fig-align="left"}

## Dataset matching {#sec-matching}

Visits from the CoLaus and OsteoLaus cohorts were aligned using a predefined visit-matching scheme, with OsteoLaus serving as the backbone dataset. OsteoLaus Baseline was paired with CoLaus Follow-up 1 (F1), OsteoLaus Visit 3 (V3) with CoLaus Follow-up 2 (F2), and OsteoLaus Visit 4 (V4) with CoLaus Follow-up 3 (F3), corresponding to study time points T1, T2, and T3, respectively (@fig-timeline). OsteoLaus Visit 2 (V2) was excluded because it had no corresponding CoLaus assessment and was not part of the longitudinal analysis framework. Similarly, the baseline visit of CoLaus was excluded. OsteoLaus Visit 5 (V5) was retained as an OsteoLaus-only assessment and defined as time point T4 to retain two time points for gait speed. <!--# All OsteoLaus observations were retained through a left-join procedure, ensuring that participants with OsteoLaus data remained in the analytical dataset even when corresponding CoLaus information was unavailable. -->

For variables available in both cohorts, the CoLaus value was preferentially retained, with the corresponding OsteoLaus value used only when the CoLaus value was missing. Variables collected exclusively in OsteoLaus, such as appendicular lean mass measurements, were retained unchanged. The final dataset contained harmonized variables together with indicators of study time point and the difference in examination dates between matched visits.

## Exposure

### Dietary assessment

Dietary intake, including dairy consumption, was assessed in the CoLaus study from the first follow-up visit onwards using a self-administered semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire (FFQ). The FFQ was developed and validated in Geneva and includes 97 food items covering intake over the previous 4 weeks [@bernstein1995; @marques-vidal2018]. Participants reported consumption frequency and portion size for each item. Portion sizes were defined as seen in @tbl-ffq for dairy products. Daily intake (g/day or mL/day) was calculated by combining frequency and portion size information. Energy and nutrient values were derived using the French CIQUAL food composition database [@ciqual].

### Total dairy intake

Total dairy intake was defined as the sum of milk, cheese, yoghurt, cream, butter, and dairy-based desserts. Intake was expressed in grams per day, assuming a density of 1 g/mL for liquid dairy products to allow harmonisation across units. Ice cream (FFQ68) was reported together with sorbet. The entire reported amount was assumed to represent a dairy-based product and was fully included in total dairy intake.

### Dairy subtypes

Dairy subtypes were derived by summing predefined FFQ items. Fermented dairy included yoghurt and cheese. Non-fermented dairy included milk, cream, and ice cream. Full-fat dairy comprised full-fat milk, yoghurt, cheese, cream, butter, and ice cream, while low-fat dairy included skimmed milk, low-fat yoghurt, and reduced-fat cheese. Detailed FFQ item mappings are provided in the supplementary material. <!--# Table S1 remember to include this -->

### Adherence to dietary guidelines

Adherence to Swiss Society for Nutrition recommendations for dairy intake was classified as meeting or not meeting recommended intake levels [@dairyguid]. Intake was calculated using weighted frequency scores based on portion size (0.5 for smaller, 1.0 for equal, 1.5 for larger portions) for selected dairy items contributing substantially to total intake (FFQ1 to FFQ8, FFQ85 and FFQ86).

### Exposure modelling

Total dairy intake was the primary exposure and was analyzed both as a continuous variable and in quartiles. Quartile cut-offs were derived from the distribution at the first follow-up visit and applied to all subsequent visits. Dairy subtypes were included in the main analysis and were modelled only as continuous variables.

For longitudinal analyses, cumulative average intake was calculated as the mean of all available previous intakes up to each visit. A lagged cumulative average (excluding the most recent visit) was used in sensitivity analyses. Additional sensitivity analyses included adherence to dietary guidelines.

## Covariates

### Covariate selection

Covariates were selected based on prior evidence of direct or indirect associations with muscle mass, physical function sarcopenia, and dairy intake. A directed acyclic graph (DAG) was used to represent the assumed relationships between variables (Supplementary Figure XX <!--# add to supplements -->). The DAG guided the selection of a minimal sufficient adjustment set to control for confounding. Variables that did not contribute to blocking confounding paths, as well as potential mediators, colliders, or redundant variables, were not included in the final models. Despite careful selection, residual confounding from unmeasured or incompletely measured factors may still be present.

### Sociodemographic

Sociodemographic factors are associated with dietary patterns and lifestyle. Therefore, these factors are also associated with health outcome. The sociodemographic variables were self-reported. This study included the following variables:

- Age of each participant was derived at each visit using the birth date and examination date.

- Educational level was defined as the highest level of education completed. This value was only assessed at CoLaus baseline. It was grouped into three categories based on the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED): low (ISCED 0-2), medium (ISCED 3), and high (ISCED 4-8) [@ISCED].

- Marital status was recorded during the CoLaus visits and included the category living alone and living in couple.

Following sociodemographic variables were not included as confounding factor. Sex and geographical location were not used since the entire cohort were females living in Lausanne, Switzerland. Ethnicity was not included since over 98% of all participants were white. Income and occupation were not included because the data were not available.

### Anthropometric factors

Higher BMI is often linked to higher energy intake and to lower muscle function. <!--# SOURCE --> Thus, BMI was considered as covariate.

Height and weight were measured using standardised protocols with a portable stadiometer (Seca 216) and electronic scale (Seca Clara 803), respectively. Measurements were taken with participants barefoot and in light clothing, with precision of 0.1 cm and 0.1 kg.

Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight divided by height squared (kg/m²) and categorised according to WHO definitions: underweight (\<18.5 kg/m²), normal weight (18.5–24.9 kg/m²), overweight (25.0–29.9 kg/m²), and obese ($\geq$ 30.0 kg/m²).

### Lifestyle

Smoking may indirectly affect muscle mass through lower levels of physical activity [@degens2015]. It may also directly contribute to muscle loss by reducing protein synthesis and increasing muscle breakdown through metabolic pathway changes. Thus, the smoking status of the participant was included as covariate. Smoking history of participants was collected through self-report. Participants were grouped into three categories:

- Current smokers: those who were actively smoking at the time of the study, regardless of how much they smoked
- Former smokers: those who had smoked in the past but had quit before the study, regardless of how long ago they quit
- Never smokers: those who had never smoked

Smoking status was recorded at each CoLaus study visit. Some reported changes were not realistic, for example, switching from never smoker to former or current smoker, or from former or current smoker to never smoker. In these cases, the “never smoker” status was changed to “former smoker”, assuming participants may have answered based on their current situation rather than their lifetime history.

Alcohol consumption is not consistently linked to lower grip strength or appendicular lean mass. However, some evidence suggests that higher intake may be associated with lower muscle mass in a dose-dependent manner [@skinner2023; @cui2019]. It was therefore included as a covariate.

Alcohol consumption was assessed using two self-reported questionnaires. The first method asked participants how many alcoholic drinks they had consumed in the previous 7 days measured in units/week and was used for the main analysis. The second method asked about the number of glasses of wine, bottles of beer, or shots of spirits consumed in the past month measured in gram ethanol/day and was used for sensitivity analyses.

Based on these responses, the number of units consumed per week was calculated. According to Swiss national guidelines, one standard drink was defined as one glass of wine, one bottle of beer, or one shot of spirits, each containing about 10 g to 12 g of pure ethanol [@standardglas]. The alcohol intake in grams per day was converted into units per week using 10 g of ethanol per unit. Participants were then grouped into four categories based on their total weekly alcohol intake:

- Non-drinkers: 0 units/week (0 g/day), which includes both lifetime and current abstainers.
- Light drinkers: $\geq$ 1 to 3 units/week (\> 0–6 g/day), representing occasional consumption.
- Moderate drinkers: $\geq$ 4 to 7 units/week (\> 6–12 g/day), representing frequent consumption within the Swiss low-risk limit for women.
- Heavy drinkers: \> 7 units/week (\> 12 g/day), categorized as hazardous consumption exceeding the Swiss national guidelines for women.

While this categorization provides a structured metric for analysis, it is noted that self-reported dietary and alcohol questionnaires often slightly underestimate absolute intake levels [@kerr2012; @morabia1994]. Validation studies in the Swiss population (Geneva) have specifically demonstrated that semi-quantitative FFQs tend to underestimate absolute alcohol consumption when compared to more intensive 24-hour recall methods [@morabia1994].

Physical activity (PA) was considered as a covariate due to extensive evidence demonstrating its strong association with muscle function outcomes in older adults. Systematic reviews and longitudinal studies consistently show that higher levels of physical activity are associated with better muscle strength, power, and functional performance in older populations [@ramsey2021; @ward-ritacco2022]

PA was measured using a Physical Activity Frequency Questionnaire (PAFQ) developed in 1998 for the Geneva population and containing 70 types of physical activity [@bernstein1998]. The questionnaire recorded how many days during the past week (0-7 days) each activity was performed and the duration per day (0-10 hours in 15-minute increments) [@verhoog2019]. Each activity was classified according to its metabolic equivalent of task (MET) value as sedentary behaviour (\< 2 METs), light physical activity (2 to \< 3 METs), moderate physical activity (3-6 METs), or vigorous physical activity (\> 6 METs).

This assessment was only available at the first and second follow-up visits of the CoLaus study. A previous study in a subpopulation of CoLaus showed a moderate correlation between physical activity measured with the PAFQ and accelerometer-based measurements [@verhoog2019]. Self-reported questionnaires tend to overestimate physical activity and underestimate sedentary behaviour. Therefore, physical activity was analyzed as tertiles representing low, moderate, and high activity levels rather than as a continuous variable. Tertiles were used because no established reference values were available.

The tertiles were defined using the combined amount of moderate and vigorous physical activity reported at the first follow-up visit and were subsequently applied to all time points. Only moderate and vigorous physical activity were used to determine level because these measures showed the smallest difference compared with accelerometer-based assessments [@verhoog2019].

### Dietary assessment

Total energy intake was assessed as a covariate to account for overall dietary quantity, since individuals with higher energy intake tend to consume more of all food groups, including dairy. Adjusting for total energy intake helps separate the association of dairy intake from overall food consumption and reduces confounding due to differences in dietary energy intake between participants. Total energy intake was calculated as the sum of all FFQ items (all 97 food items), using energy values derived from the French CIQUAL food composition table [@ciqual].

<!--#  Dietary food groups were derived from the FFQ for use in marginal structural models to account for overall dietary patterns and potential time-varying confounding. Individual FFQ items were aggregated into predefined food groups based on nutritional similarity. Food groups included animal protein (meat, fish, seafood, and eggs), plant protein (tofu), vegetables, fruits, grains, fats and oils, processed foods, and alcohol. For each participant, daily intake (g/day) was calculated by summing the intake of all FFQ items within each group. If any contributing item was missing, the corresponding food group was set to missing to avoid partial aggregation bias.-->

### Clinical

Type 2 diabetes was assessed as a covariate because previous studies have shown a bidirectional relationship between diabetes and sarcopenia. Diabetes may contribute to reduced muscle mass and function through insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and altered protein metabolism, while low muscle mass may also worsen glucose metabolism and increase diabetes risk [@chen2023].

Diabetes status was assessed using three sources all recorded during CoLaus visits: self-report, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), and glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c). Self-report was based on the question “Have you ever been told that you had diabetes?”. Among the objective measures, HbA1c was considered the primary indicator due to its higher reliability and was used whenever available. If HbA1c was missing, FPG was used. If neither biomarker was available, diabetes status was based on self-report. Description of the sample collection procedure can be found elsewhere [@ducraux2021].

Hormonal replacement therapy (HRT) status was assessed for a potential covariate because previous research shows mixed but biologically plausible effects on muscle outcomes in postmenopausal women [@xu2020]. Given the variability in HRT use among participants, controlling for this factor helps ensure observed associations are not influenced by hormonal differences.

HRT use was assessed using self-reported questionnaire data. Participants were asked whether they were currently using HRT and at what age HRT was started. Based on these responses, HRT status was classified into three categories: current HRT use, past HRT use, and never/not current HRT use. Participants who answered “Yes” to current HRT use were classified as current users. Participants who answered “No” but provided a valid age at HRT initiation were classified as past users. Participants who answered “No” and had no indication of previous HRT use were classified as never/not current users. HRT status was set to missing when information on current HRT use was unavailable.

Hypertension was considered as covariant because of the established association between hypertension and reduced muscle mass [@han2020]. Hypertension status was derived using a hierarchical approach based on three sources of information: measured hypertension, documented antihypertensive treatment, and self-reported antihypertensive medication use. Measured hypertension was defined as systolic blood pressure $\geq$ 140 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure $\geq$ 90 mmHg and was considered the primary source. Participants were classified as having hypertension if measured hypertension was present. If measured hypertension data were missing, documented antihypertensive treatment was used. If both measured hypertension and documented treatment data were unavailable, self-reported antihypertensive medication use was considered. Participants were classified as not having hypertension when at least one data source was available and none indicated hypertension. Hypertension status was set to missing when all three sources were unavailable.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is associated with reduced muscle mass and function through multiple mechanisms, including reduced physical activity due to symptoms such as fatigue and dyspnoea, impaired muscle perfusion and oxygen delivery, systemic inflammation, and shared metabolic risk factors such as insulin resistance and age-related pathways. <!--# SOURCE. -->

CVD event status was derived as a composite binary variable (any CVD event: yes/no) based on 13 self-reported and clinically reported cardiovascular conditions, including myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, coronary artery disease, angina, cardiomyopathy, cardiac surgery, heart valve surgery, treated arrhythmia, peripheral vascular surgery, cardiac catheterisation, coronary artery bypass graft, and percutaneous coronary intervention.

Participants were classified as having a CVD event if at least one of the component conditions was reported as “Yes”. Participants were classified as having no CVD event if at least one component was available, and all reported conditions were “No”. Participants were classified as missing if no information was available across all component variables. CVD status was available only at baseline.

### Medication and supplement use

The use of prescribed medication and supplements was assessed by self-report during CoLaus visits. Each drug type is descried with the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) Classification. Some drugs have beneficial effects on muscle mass and muscle function, whereas others negatively impact muscle related outcomes.

Lipid-lowering medications have been linked to muscle-related adverse effects in clinical reports [@shin2026]. However, evidence for an association with reduced muscle mass or impaired muscle function remains inconsistent, with some studies reporting negative associations [@shin2026] and others finding no effect [@fazel2026]. Lipid-lowering drugs were defined as all medications classified under ATC code C10.

Evidence indicates systemic corticosteroid use \[SOURCE\] and benzodiazepines \[SOURCE\] negatively impact muscle strength, mass, and functional outcomes in older adults. Thus, ATC codes starting with H02 were included for systemic corticosteroid use and N05B for benzodiazepines use.

The evidence for muscle protective effects of bisphosphonate use in humans is limited, but it was suggested that bone-to-muscle paracrine signalling may mediate benefits [@klein2018]. Therefore, all participants reporting ACT codes with M05BA were considered to take bisphosphonate.

Vitamin D supplementation (ACT code A11) and calcium supplementation (ACT code A12A) are positively associated with muscle outcomes [@gao2026]. These variables are included as covariates in the analysis.

## Outcome Variables

### Handgrip strength

Handgrip strength (HGS) was measured in all CoLaus visits using a JAMAR Baseline® hydraulic hand dynamometer (Fabrication Enterprises, Inc., White Plains, NY, USA) following the guidelines of the American Society of Hand Therapists. Values were recorded in pounds and converted to kilograms using a conversion factor of 0.454.

In OsteoLaus, HGS was assessed only at visit V5 using the same protocol. The highest value from three attempts of the dominant hand was used for analysis. Measurements were recorded directly in kilograms. Further details of the procedure are described in Vendrami et al. (2025) [@vendrami2025].

### Appendicular lean mass

Appendicular lean mass (ALM) was defined as the sum of lean mass of the arms and legs. ALM was measured at all five OsteoLaus visits using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Two devices were used over time: the Hologic Horizon A System™ for the first two visits and the GE Lunar iDXA™ system for the remaining visits.

A study within the same cohort revealed that the Hologic Horizon A System generally leads to a higher lean mass (1293.7 g ± 1643.5 g) [@vendrami2024]. However, the lean mass of the arms and legs are higher for the Lunar iDXA device (arms 151.4 g ± 274.8 g; legs: 777.1 g ± 490.0 g).

Because systematic differences were observed between devices, ALM values were harmonised using previously published cross-calibration equations derived within the same OsteoLaus cohort [@vendrami2024]. Hologic-derived values were converted to Lunar-equivalent values prior to analysis using the following equation: $ALM_{Holigic}=−369.3+0.967\cdot ALM_{Lunar}$

Appendicular lean mass index (ALMI) was calculated as ALM divided by height squared (kg/m²). ALM was converted from grams to kilograms and height from centimetres to metres before calculation.

Sensitivity analyses additionally included alternative muscle mass indices based on ALM adjusted for body mass index (ALM/BMI) and ALM adjusted for height squared (ALM/height²)

### Gait speed

Gait speed (GS) was used as a measure of physical performance and functional capacity. It was assessed using a 6-metre walk test performed at usual walking pace and expressed in metres per second (m/s). Detailed procedures are described in Vendrami et al. [@vendrami2025]. Slow gait speed was defined as $≤$ 0.8 m/s.

### Sarcopenia

Sarcopenia was defined according to the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People 2 (EWGSOP2) criteria [@cruz-jentoft2019] and used for the main analyses. Muscle strength was defined as low when HGS was \<16 kg, muscle mass as low when ALMI was \<5.5 kg/m², and physical performance as low when gait speed was $≤$ 0.8 m/s. These are the female-specific thresholds of EWGSOP2 sarcopenia definition.

Participants were classified into four categories: no sarcopenia, probable sarcopenia (low muscle strength only), confirmed sarcopenia (low muscle strength and low muscle mass), and severe sarcopenia (low muscle strength, low muscle mass, and low physical performance). Gait speed was only available at visits T3 and T4. Therefore, severe sarcopenia could not be assessed at earlier visits. This limitation did not affect the primary sarcopenia classification, as participants were classified as sarcopenic if they met criteria for either confirmed or severe sarcopenia.

In sensitivity analyses, sarcopenia was additionally defined using the Foundation for the National Institutes of Health (FNIH) criteria [@studenski2014], based on the combination of low muscle strength (HGS \<16 kg) and low muscle mass relative to body mass index (ALM/BMI \<0.512). Participants were classified as having sarcopenia or no sarcopenia under this definition.

## Statistical Methods

All analyses were performed in R version 4.5.1 [@Rprogram]. Data preparation and manipulation was done with dplyr (version 1.2.0) [@wickham2026]. Results were visualised using ggplot2 (version 4.0.2) [@wickham2016a] For descriptive analyses, participants were grouped into quartiles based on baseline daily total dairy intake (g/day). Categorical variables are presented as counts and percentages, and continuous variables as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or median with interquartile range (IQR), as appropriate.

### Missing data

Missing data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) implemented in the R package mice (version 3.19.0) [@buuren2011]. Imputation was performed under a fully conditional specification framework and with the assumption that data were missing at random.

Longitudinal data were reshaped into wide format (one row per participant with separate columns for each visit), allowing within-person correlations across time to be incorporated in the imputation model. A total of 20 imputed datasets were generated (m = 20), with 20 iterations per dataset.

<!--# add that participants with more than 80% missing values were not imputed since it would lead to unreliable imputation and imputed values would be highly model-dependent -->

Continuous variables were imputed using predictive mean matching <!--# taking d=10 example complete cases instead of 5 which is standard -->. Binary variables were imputed using logistic regression, and ordinal variables using proportional odds models. Derived variables were not imputed directly. Instead, they were recomputed after imputation from the underlying variables. This approach preserves internal consistency between raw and derived variables. Auxiliary variables (e.g. participant identifiers and examination dates) were included as predictors to improve imputation accuracy but were not themselves imputed. <!--# why? -->

For OsteoLaus, visit structure and measurement design were explicitly incorporated. Variables were only imputed at visits where measurement was possible (e.g. gait speed only at T3 and T4). For DXA-derived variables, measurements obtained from different devices were prevented from directly predicting each other to reduce systematic bias across measurement methods.

Predictor matrices were manually specified to preserve temporal structure. Only missing values were imputed. Observed values were left unchanged. Post-imputation diagnostics included trace plots, density plots, and strip plots to assess convergence and distributional plausibility across imputations.

<!--#  In addition, numerical range checks were performed on imputed datasets to identify implausible values. -->

### Data cleaning and exclusions

Data cleaning was performed sequentially using predefined quality control criteria. First, participants were excluded if they failed study-level quality checks. These included inconsistent participant identifiers, missing or invalid examination dates, sex inconsistencies across visits, and implausible age trajectories over time. Second, visit-level observations were excluded if required exposure, outcome, or covariate data were missing after imputation and harmonisation steps.

Visit dates and temporal alignment CoLaus visits consisted of two separate assessments: a physical examination and a questionnaire assessment. These assessments were not always performed on the same day, although they usually took place within a few days of each other. Age was originally calculated using the participant’s birth date and the questionnaire examination date. However, these dates were not available for the present study. Therefore, the physical examination date was used as the temporal reference for linking CoLaus and OsteoLaus visits, as described in @sec-matching. In some cases, participants completed the questionnaire assessment but did not attend the physical examination, resulting in a missing physical examination date. For these visits, an estimated physical examination date was derived using the available examination date from another visit together with the difference in calculated age between visits. This approach assumed that the questionnaire and physical examination were conducted within a short time interval.

Data cleaning of outcome, exposure, and covariate variables is described above in the corresponding sections above.

Range-based plausibility checks were then applied. Total energy intake was restricted to 500–3500 <!--# check number --> kcal/day. <!--# SOURCE --> HGS values were required to be \>0 kg, and total dairy intake was restricted to 0–1500 g/day. <!--# justification --> For analyses with sarcopenia as the outcome, participants with prevalent sarcopenia at baseline were excluded to ensure incident case analyses. Under the EWGSOP2 definition, participants were excluded if baseline sarcopenia status was missing or if they were classified as having sarcopenia (“confirmed” or “severe”). Under the FNIH definition, participants were excluded if baseline sarcopenia status was missing or if sarcopenia was present at baseline. Finally, participants were required to contribute at least two <!--# is it 2? -->valid study visits to be included in longitudinal analyses.

### Covariate selection

Covariates were selected a priori based on existing evidence and a DAG to identify a sufficient adjustment set.

- Handgrip strength**:** Age, BMI, diabetes, education, physical activity, smoking status, total energy intake

- Appendicular lean mass index: Age, BMI, diabetes, education, physical activity, smoking status, total energy intake

- Gait speed: Age, BMI, diabetes, education, physical activity, smoking status

- Sarcopenia**:** Age, BMI, diabetes, education, physical activity, smoking status

Variables were excluded from final models if they were identified as mediators, colliders, redundant measures, or not required to block confounding pathways according to the DAG.

### Linear mixed-effects models

Linear mixed-effects models were fitted using the lmerTest package (version 3.2-1) in R [@kuznetsova2017]. These models were used to analyse repeated measurements over time while accounting for within-participant correlation, and to assess how changes in exposure were associated with changes in outcomes over time.

Age was modelled using two separate variables: age at baseline and time since baseline. Age at baseline was included to account for differences in participant age at study entry, while time since baseline represented within-person change over follow-up. Chronological age was not included directly because it is mathematically dependent on baseline age and follow-up time, which would lead to collinearity in the model. This approach allowed separation of cross-sectional age differences from longitudinal changes over time.

All continuous covariates were mean-centred prior to model fitting. This improves numerical stability and convergence while keeping coefficients interpretable in their original units. Categorical variables were recoded with predefined reference categories to ensure consistent interpretation of effect estimates across models.

The models included fixed effects for the exposure, time (visit), and selected covariates. To account for within-individual correlation across repeated measurements, random intercepts for participants were included in all models. Models were extended with random slopes to allowed for individual-specific trajectories over time.

For multiple imputed data, models were fitted within each imputed dataset and pooled using Rubin’s rules via the mice package. <!--# source --> Fixed-effect estimates were extracted using standard mixed-model summary procedures and reported as regression coefficients with 95% confidence intervals.

<!--# We report clubSandwich CR2 robust standard errors as our primary inference, as they are robust to heteroscedasticity and misspecification of the random effects. Standard LMM SEs are provided for comparison in the appendix. -->

### **Cox proportional hazards model**

Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to examine the association between dairy intake and incident sarcopenia. The package survival (version 3.8.3) was used [@therneau2026]. Sarcopenia was defined according to either the EWGSOP2 [@cruz-jentoft2019] or FNIH criteria [@studenski2014] and analyzed as a binary outcome. Participants were followed from baseline until the first occurrence of sarcopenia or until their last available follow-up visit, whichever occurred first.

Two modelling approaches were applied. In the baseline model, each participant contributed a single observation, and covariates were taken from the baseline visit only. In the time-dependent model, participants contributed repeated observations across follow-up visits, allowing exposure and covariate values to be updated over time. Age was used as the underlying time scale in all models.

Dairy intake was modelled a continuous variable (grams per day). To reduce the risk of model overfitting, BMI was modelled as continuous variables where appropriate rather than categorical variables. Categorising continuous variables increases the number of model parameters and therefore the degrees of freedom required for estimation. Because the number of incident sarcopenia cases was limited (89 events among 1317 participants) <!--# adjust to exact numbers -->, restricting the number of parameters was important to maintain model stability and reduce the risk of overfitting. Previous methodological work has shown that regression models with a low number of events per parameter can produce unstable and overly optimistic estimates that may not replicate in other samples [@babyak2004]. Modelling variables continuously preserves statistical power, retains the full information contained in the data, and reduces unnecessary parameter estimation.

Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using partial likelihood estimation with Efron’s method to account for tied event times. For analyses based on multiply imputed datasets, models were fitted separately within each imputed dataset and pooled using Rubin’s rules. <!--# source -->

Model assumptions were assessed for the fully adjusted models. The proportional hazards assumption was evaluated using Schoenfeld residuals and global proportional hazards tests. Functional form was assessed using martingale residuals, while influential observations were examined using deviance residuals and standardised DFBETA statistics. Multicollinearity among covariates was assessed using variance inflation factors. <!--# add package car if reported --> Kaplan-Meier curves were generated for categorical dairy intake models to visualise differences in sarcopenia-free survival across exposure groups. <!--# add all necessariy packages used for this -->

<!--# Inverse probability of treatment weights (IPTW) were estimated using the WeightIt package. IPCW models included age category, sex, occupation, BMI category, smoking status, cardiovascular events, hypertension, depression, physical activity, education, and family income. Participant identifiers were specified using the id argument, and an independence working correlation structure was used (corstr = "independence"). The resulting coefficients therefore represented marginal population-average causal effect estimates under the weighted pseudo-population. -->

## Ethics

CoLaus \textbar{} PsyCoLaus and the OsteoLaus studies were approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of the University of Lausanne. All participants signed a written informed consent form after having received a detailed description of the goal and funding of the studies.

## Data and Code Availability Statement

This observational cohort study is reported in accordance with the STROBE guidelines [@STROBE].

The data used in this study are not publicly available but may be requested subject to approval. More information on data request can be found [www.colaus-psycolaus.ch](www.colaus-psycolaus.ch).

All code used for data processing and statistical analyses is available on GitHub: <https://github.com/ann4boss/OsteoLaus-Dairy-Sarcopenia>.
